section.title: The Treaty at Beersheba
section.sectionRationale: Right after God has vindicated Sarah and provided for Hagar's son, a pagan king comes seeking a treaty because he can see that God is with Abraham. The wandering sojourner secures a foothold in the land, a well and a name, and worships the Eternal God.
section.thesis: The nations begin to recognise that God is with Abraham; the pilgrim who owns nothing makes peace, secures a well, and calls on the LORD as the Everlasting God who keeps His promises.
section.frameNote: Three scenes: Abimelech asks for an oath; the dispute over a seized well; peace, a name for the place, and worship at Beersheba.

units.label: Abimelech seeks an oath
units.note: God is with you in all that you do

verses.text: At that time Abimelech and Phicol the commander of his army said to Abraham, “God is with you in all that you do.

Now, therefore, {{swear|swear}} to me here before God that you will not deal falsely with me or my children or descendants. Show to me and to the country in which you reside the same kindness that I have shown to you.”
But when Abraham complained to Abimelech about a well that Abimelech’s servants had seized,
Abimelech replied, “I do not know who has done this. You did not tell me, so I have not heard about it until today.”
So Abraham brought sheep and cattle and gave them to Abimelech, and the two men made a {{covenant|covenant}}.
Abraham separated seven ewe lambs from the flock,
and Abimelech asked him, “Why have you set apart these seven ewe lambs?”
He replied, “You are to accept the seven ewe lambs from my hand as my witness that I dug this well.”
So that place was called {{beersheba|Beersheba}}, because it was there that the two of them swore an oath.
After they had made the covenant at Beersheba, Abimelech and Phicol the commander of his army got up and returned to the land of the Philistines.
And Abraham planted a tamarisk tree in Beersheba, and there he called upon the name of the LORD, {{elolam|the Eternal God}}.
And Abraham resided in the land of the Philistines for a long time.

swear.gloss: To swear an oath or bind oneself by solemn promise. The verb is built on the number seven, and to swear is literally to seven oneself. Oaths in Genesis are weighty acts taken before God as witness, and here they turn a tense relationship into a lasting peace.

covenant.gloss: A binding agreement or treaty, often sealed with a sign or a sacrifice. Between Abraham and Abimelech it is a peace pact between neighbours. The same word carries the far greater bond God Himself makes with Abraham, and finally the new covenant sealed in the blood of Christ.

beersheba.gloss: A place name meaning well of seven or well of the oath. It marks both the seven lambs given as witness and the oath sworn there. Beersheba becomes a settled landmark of the patriarchs and a standing memorial that God gave Abraham a foothold in the land of promise.

elolam.gloss: A title for God meaning the Everlasting or Eternal God. Olam speaks of unbounded, age long duration. Abraham worships the God who does not change or pass away, the fitting anchor for a man who owns almost nothing but holds an everlasting promise.

basic.context: Abraham is still a resident foreigner in Canaan, owning no land. A local king, Abimelech, comes with his army commander to make a peace treaty because he can see that God blesses everything Abraham does. Along the way Abraham raises a complaint about a well his men had seized. The key question is what it looks like for God's promise to start bearing fruit even before Abraham owns the land.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a narrative about real events, not a set of commands. It shows the promise of Genesis 12, that Abraham would be a blessing to the nations, beginning to come true as a pagan king seeks him out. The interpreter should read it as one more step in God keeping His word, not as a rule for treaty making.
basic.originalLanguages: The scene turns on oaths: to swear, shaba, is tied to the number seven, and Abraham sets apart seven ewe lambs at the place he names Beersheba, the well of the oath. The two men cut a covenant, berith. At the end Abraham worships El Olam, the Everlasting God, the God whose promises outlast every human treaty.
basic.typology: Abraham the sojourner gaining a secure well and a place of worship is a small foretaste of the inheritance God has promised. It points ahead to the people of God who, though pilgrims now, will receive a lasting home. The well of living water anticipates the water Christ gives that never runs dry.
basic.christ: Abimelech recognises that God is with Abraham, an early sign of the nations being drawn to the line through which Christ will come. The Everlasting God whom Abraham calls upon is the same God fully revealed in Jesus, who makes lasting peace not by a bargain but by His own blood.
basic.god: God is faithful and present: His visible blessing on Abraham is what draws Abimelech. He is the Everlasting God, unchanging, who can be trusted to keep a promise across generations. He gives His pilgrim people footholds of grace along the way.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 12 promised blessing to the nations through Abraham, and here a king seeks him out. Hebrews 11 calls Abraham a stranger who looked for a lasting city. Isaiah 40 celebrates the Everlasting God who does not grow weary.
basic.oneStory: The wandering man of promise makes peace, secures a well, and worships the Eternal God. It is a quiet scene, but it shows God beginning to fulfil His pledge to bless the world through Abraham, the line that runs all the way to Christ.

context.literary:
The scene is framed by an arrival and a departure. 'Abimelech and Phicol the commander of his army' come to Abraham in verse 22, and the same pair, named in the same words, 'got up and returned to the land of the Philistines' in verse 32. Inside that frame the dialogue moves in three steps. Abimelech asks for an oath and Abraham gives it at once, verses 22 to 24. Abraham then raises a grievance over a well, and a covenant is made with a gift of flocks, verses 25 to 27. Finally seven ewe lambs are set apart as a witness and the place is named, verses 28 to 31. After the visitors leave, the camera stays on Abraham alone, planting, calling on the LORD, and staying, verses 33 and 34.

The vocabulary of oath and number binds the scene together. The root for swearing and the number seven sound alike in Hebrew, and they alternate through the passage: swear, I swear, seven ewe lambs three times over, and then the name Beersheba, which the BSB footnote explains as 'well of seven or well of the oath.' The name holds both meanings at once, and the narrator leaves both in play.

The passage belongs to its setting in chapter 21 and beyond. It opens 'At that time,' tying it to the birth of Isaac and the departure of Ishmael. It also completes the story of Abimelech begun in chapter 20. There the king had been wronged by Abraham's deceit; here he asks Abraham to deal truly with him, and the man whose word was doubtful in Gerar gives his oath. There Abimelech offered 'my land is before you,' Genesis 20:15; here Abraham secures a single well in it.

The closing verses are quiet by design. They set a peaceful stillness, a tree, a name, a long stay, before the words 'Some time later God tested Abraham,' Genesis 22:1. Abraham returns to Beersheba after Moriah, Genesis 22:19, so this well becomes the home base of the greatest test of his life.
context.historical:
Abimelech comes with Phicol, 'the commander of his army,' verse 22. A king who brings his general to a negotiation is not paying a social call. Abraham had become a wealthy chief with a large household of servants, enough to field fighting men, as Genesis 14:14 had already shown. From the king's side, the treaty secures peace with a powerful neighbour for the next generations: 'me or my children or descendants,' verse 23.

Water was the heart of the matter. In the Negev, where rainfall is slight, a dug well was a major investment of labour and a claim to use the land around it for grazing. Seizing one, verse 25, was a serious wrong; the verb is the ordinary word for robbery. The later history of these same wells shows how contested they were: after Abraham's death the Philistines stopped them up with dirt, and Isaac's herdsmen fought over new ones, Genesis 26:15-21.

The transaction follows familiar ancient forms. Gifts of livestock accompany the covenant, verse 27. Then a separate gift of seven ewe lambs serves as legal evidence, verse 30: if Abimelech accepts them, he acknowledges before witnesses that Abraham dug the well. Physical witnesses to agreements recur in Genesis, as with the heap of stones Jacob and Laban set up, Genesis 31:44-48.

The tamarisk, verse 33, is a hardy tree of dry country, able to live long and give shade where little else grows. Planting a tree is an act of someone who expects to stay.

The phrase 'the land of the Philistines,' verses 32 and 34, raises a historical question. The Philistines known from later Israelite history settled on the southern coast in the early Iron Age, well after the patriarchal period. Either the narrator uses the later name for the region, or Abimelech's people were an earlier group of related origin. The modern city of Beer Sheva still carries the name Abraham gave.
context.canonical:
Beersheba becomes a landmark of the whole patriarchal story. Isaac later reaches it after the quarrels over wells, receives God's promise there, builds an altar, and makes a similar treaty with an Abimelech and a Phicol, naming a well Shibah, 'and to this day the name of the city is Beersheba,' Genesis 26:23-33. Jacob sets out from Beersheba for Haran, Genesis 28:10, and returns to offer sacrifices there before going down to Egypt, where God says, 'Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt,' Genesis 46:1-3.

Later, 'from Dan to Beersheba' becomes Israel's way of saying the whole land, north to south, Judges 20:1 and 1 Samuel 3:20. Samuel's sons judge there, 1 Samuel 8:2, and Elijah flees there from Jezebel, 1 Kings 19:3. By Amos's day the place of Abraham's worship had become a pilgrimage site for corrupt religion: 'do not journey to Beersheba,' Amos 5:5, and the people swore 'As surely as the way of Beersheba lives,' Amos 8:14. A place hallowed by true worship could become an idol.

The title El Olam is echoed wherever Scripture praises God's eternity. 'From everlasting to everlasting You are God,' Psalm 90:2. 'The LORD is the everlasting God, the Creator of the ends of the earth,' Isaiah 40:28. 'The eternal God is your dwelling place,' Deuteronomy 33:27. Paul speaks of 'the command of the eternal God' that leads 'all nations to the obedience that comes from faith,' Romans 16:26.

Scripture also takes oaths with Gentiles seriously. Israel's leaders were bound by their oath to the Gibeonites, Joshua 9:19, and when Saul broke it, famine followed, 2 Samuel 21:1-2. The New Testament recalls Abraham as a man who 'dwelt in the promised land as a stranger,' Hebrews 11:9, which is exactly the picture this passage paints.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to see the promise of Genesis 12:2-3 at work in ordinary life. A king who had every political advantage came to a landless herdsman and said, 'God is with you in all that you do,' verse 22. The blessing on Abraham was visible enough to be recognised by outsiders and weighty enough to change their policy.

He also wanted them to see how the chosen family should live among the nations while the promise was still unfulfilled. Abraham does not seize land. He negotiates, raises a grievance openly rather than by force, makes a sworn agreement, and pays to have his rights recognised. The land promised to him by God is not taken by violence in Genesis; the patriarchs live as sojourners and deal honourably with their neighbours.

Finally, he wanted Israel to see where Abraham placed his confidence. The treaty secured peace for Abimelech's 'children or descendants,' verse 23. Abraham's response is to worship El Olam, verse 33, the God whose commitments reach far beyond three generations. The well and the treaty were gifts for the present. The hope of the future rested on the eternal God.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage records a treaty and an act of worship; it gives no command to repeat them. Believers are not told to seal agreements with seven lambs or to plant trees where they pray. The planting of a tree beside a place of worship later became dangerous in Israel, and the law forbade setting up an Asherah pole next to the LORD's altar, Deuteronomy 16:21, so this detail is not a pattern to copy.

What does carry over is the character of the man and of his God. Abraham keeps his word, 'I swear it,' verse 24, and raises his complaint honestly instead of taking revenge, a pattern the New Testament commends: 'If it is possible on your part, live at peace with everyone,' Romans 12:18. He lets the visible blessing of God speak for him among outsiders, as Peter urges believers to do so that others 'may see your good deeds and glorify God,' 1 Peter 2:12. And he calls on the name of the LORD wherever he settles, as every believer may.

debates.question: Is Abimelech's treaty a sign of God's blessing on Abraham or merely shrewd politics by a nervous neighbour?

views.label: A fruit of God's blessing
views.case: Abimelech openly says 'God is with you in all that you do,' verse 22, echoing the promise of Genesis 12:2-3. Having seen God act on Abraham's behalf in Genesis 20, the king seeks his favour, and the narrator frames the scene as blessing recognised by the nations.

views.label: Political self interest
views.case: Abimelech brings his army commander and asks for protection for his descendants, verse 23. He is securing peace with a powerful neighbour whose household was large enough to be a threat, a natural act of statecraft that need not carry deep theological weight.

debates.bearing: Both can be true at once. God's blessing is real, and it is precisely that visible blessing that moves a self interested king to seek peace, which is how the promise to bless the nations often works out on the ground.

debates.question: How should we understand 'the land of the Philistines' in verses 32 and 34?

views.label: A later name for the region
views.case: The Philistines known from Israel's later history arrived on the coast in the early Iron Age. On this view the narrator, writing for later readers, uses the name they knew for the territory around Gerar, just as Genesis elsewhere explains older names with later ones.

views.label: An earlier related people
views.case: Others argue that groups from the Aegean world were trading and settling on the coast long before the major Philistine settlement, and that Abimelech's people could be an early community of this kind. They note that Abimelech behaves very differently from the later Philistine city states.

debates.bearing: The question concerns the historical label, not the event. Either way the narrator locates Abraham among the people who would later be among Israel's fiercest enemies, and shows that the father of Israel lived at peace with them by oath.

debates.question: Why does Abraham plant a tamarisk tree at Beersheba?

views.label: A mark of permanence
views.case: A tamarisk grows slowly and lives long. Planting one beside a secured well says that Abraham expects his household to stay, and it serves as a visible marker of the covenant just made.

views.label: A place of worship
views.case: The planting is joined directly to calling on the name of the LORD, verse 33. Abraham had earlier worshipped by the Oaks of Mamre, Genesis 13:18, and a tree could mark a place where God was invoked, before Israel's law forbade trees beside the altar.

debates.bearing: The two readings fit together. The tree marks both settled presence and worship, a pledge of hope in the land and a memorial of the name called on there. What Scripture stresses is not the tree but the God invoked beside it.

study.originalLanguages:
Beyond oath, covenant and the Everlasting God, several words in the passage are worth close attention.

Abimelech asks Abraham to show him 'the same kindness,' verse 23, and the word is chesed, loyal love, the faithful kindness that keeps a relationship. It is the very word Abraham used in Genesis 20:13 when he asked Sarah to show him 'loyalty' by calling him her brother. There chesed was bent toward deceit; here a pagan king appeals to Abraham's chesed and receives an honest oath. The word will run through the Old Testament as a description of God's covenant love.

The king's concern stretches over generations: 'me or my children or descendants,' verse 23. The last two words, nin and neched, are a rhyming pair for offspring and posterity, found together again in Job 18:19 and Isaiah 14:22, where their loss means a family wiped from memory. Abimelech is thinking about his dynasty.

He speaks of 'the country in which you reside,' verse 23, using gur, to live as a resident alien, and the chapter ends with the same verb: 'Abraham resided in the land of the Philistines for a long time,' verse 34. The related noun ger is Abraham's own description of himself at Sarah's grave, 'I am a foreigner and an outsider among you,' Genesis 23:4. The passage begins and ends by reminding us that the heir of the land is still a sojourner in it.

In verse 25 Abraham 'complained,' from yakach, a legal verb for bringing a charge or setting a matter right. It is the verb Abimelech had used in Genesis 20:16 when he told Sarah she was 'completely cleared.' The well had been 'seized,' gazal, the verb for robbery that the law later forbids, 'You must not defraud your neighbor or rob him,' Leviticus 19:13.

The 'ewe lambs,' kivsot, are female lambs, the breeding stock of a flock and so of real value. They are to be a 'witness,' verse 30, using a feminine form of the noun for testimony. The lambs become legal evidence; once Abimelech receives them, he cannot later deny whose well it is.

The men 'made a covenant,' verses 27 and 32, literally cut a covenant, the idiom used of God's covenant with Abram in Genesis 15:18, where animals were cut in two.

Finally, El Olam. The noun olam refers to a long duration, reaching back into the distant past or forward without end, and so often means forever. It appears already in God's promises: an 'everlasting covenant' and an 'eternal possession,' Genesis 17:7-8. The God who made a covenant olam with Abraham is Himself El Olam. Abraham 'called upon the name,' qara beshem, the phrase first used in Genesis 4:26 when 'men began to call upon the name of the LORD,' and used of Abraham at Bethel, Genesis 12:8 and 13:4. Wherever Abraham settles, he proclaims and invokes the LORD.

typology.type: The well secured by oath at Beersheba
typology.fulfillment: A landless pilgrim gains one sure thing in the land of promise: water, guaranteed by oath. Jesus sits by another patriarchal well and offers a woman water that will become 'a fount of water springing up to eternal life,' John 4:14. The escalation is clear. Abraham's well had to be defended by treaty and was later stopped up by enemies, Genesis 26:15; the water Christ gives cannot be seized or blocked. The type also falls short in scope: Abraham's well served one household in one place, while Christ's living water is offered to all who are thirsty, John 7:37.

typology.type: A Gentile king seeking peace because God is with Abraham
typology.fulfillment: Abimelech comes to Abraham because he can see that 'God is with you.' The prophets foresee the nations coming the same way: 'ten men from the nations of every tongue will tightly grasp the robe of a Jew, saying, Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you,' Zechariah 8:23. The pattern begins to be fulfilled when Magi from the east come seeking 'the One who has been born King of the Jews,' Matthew 2:2, and in Christ, whose very name is 'God with us,' Matthew 1:23. Abimelech sought a treaty for safety; the nations come to Christ for reconciliation with God.

typology.type: Worship of the Everlasting God by a sojourner in a land not yet owned
typology.fulfillment: Abraham plants a tree and calls on El Olam while still a resident alien, verse 34. The church lives the same way, 'as foreigners and exiles,' 1 Peter 2:11, worshipping now while waiting for the inheritance. Hebrews joins the two: 'here we do not have a permanent city, but we are looking for the city that is to come,' and so 'let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise,' Hebrews 13:14-15. The escalation is that believers call on the name of the Lord Jesus, through whom the Everlasting God is known as Father. The type is limited, since Abraham looked forward dimly to what the church now sees clearly.

study.christ:
The first link to Christ is Abimelech's confession: 'God is with you in all that you do,' verse 22. It is one of the earliest times an outsider recognises God's presence with the chosen family, and it foreshadows the name given to Abraham's greatest descendant, 'Immanuel,' which means 'God with us,' Matthew 1:23. In Abraham, God's presence was visible in blessing on his flocks and household. In Jesus, God's presence is personal: God Himself has come to dwell with His people. The nations who once sought peace with Abraham because God was with him now find peace with God through the One who is God with us.

The second link is peace between enemies. Abraham makes a covenant with a king whose people would later be among Israel's bitterest foes. The peace here is limited and political, and it rests on an exchange of gifts and oaths. Christ makes a deeper peace. 'He Himself is our peace, who has made the two one and has torn down the dividing wall of hostility,' Ephesians 2:14. He reconciles all things to God, 'making peace through the blood of His cross,' Colossians 1:20. Abraham gave lambs as a witness; Christ gave Himself, and His blood seals 'the eternal covenant,' Hebrews 13:20.

The third link is water. The oath secured a well for Abraham's flocks in a dry land. Jesus, speaking at the well of Jacob, says that 'everyone who drinks this water will be thirsty again,' but whoever drinks the water He gives 'will never thirst,' John 4:13-14. The patriarch's well was valuable enough to fight over; the Messiah's water is given freely.

The fourth link is the life of the sojourner. Abraham called on the LORD in a land where he owned nothing but a well. The Son of Man had 'no place to lay His head,' Matthew 8:20, and suffered 'outside the city gate,' Hebrews 13:12. He lived as a stranger in His own world, and so His people 'go to Him outside the camp,' Hebrews 13:13, content to be pilgrims because their inheritance is secure in Him.

Finally, El Olam is not a different God from the God of the gospel. 'Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever,' Hebrews 13:8. The eternal God whom Abraham invoked at Beersheba is the God revealed in the eternal Son.

These links are drawn from the New Testament's own themes and should not be pressed further. The seven lambs are not a code for the cross, and the tamarisk is not a picture of anything. The passage points to Christ by showing what God is doing through Abraham, a blessing that reaches the nations, peace with outsiders, provision in a dry land, and worship of the eternal God, all of which come to their fullness in Jesus.
study.god:
The passage presents God first as the God whose presence can be seen. Abimelech has no covenant with Him, yet he can tell that 'God is with you in all that you do,' verse 22. God's blessing on His people is not invisible or merely private. It becomes a testimony that outsiders notice, sometimes before the chosen family does.

He is the God before whom oaths are taken. 'Swear to me here before God,' verse 23. Even a pagan king assumes that an oath before God binds more tightly than a mere promise, because God sees and judges. Laban and Jacob later say the same: 'God is a witness between you and me,' Genesis 31:50. God's truthfulness underlies all human trust, and Scripture treats an oath before Him as sacred even when made with foreigners, Joshua 9:19.

He is El Olam, the Everlasting God. This is the heart of the passage theologically. Abimelech's treaty looks ahead to his children and descendants, perhaps three generations. God's commitments are olam, reaching past every horizon. He had already promised an 'everlasting covenant' and an 'eternal possession,' Genesis 17:7-8, and here Abraham names the God who can keep such promises. The One who 'inhabits eternity,' Isaiah 57:15, is not bound by the lifespan of kings. Because He does not change, His people are not destroyed, Malachi 3:6.

His eternity is not distance. The Everlasting God is also the God with Abraham in all he does, near enough to bless his flocks and his wells. Isaiah holds both together: the One who inhabits eternity dwells also 'with the oppressed and humble in spirit.' The God of endless ages is present in a single well and a single tree.

The passage holds a tension that runs through Abraham's life. God had promised the whole land, and after all these years Abraham owns only the right to one well. Yet he worships. God's timescale is not ours, and He gives footholds of grace along the way as pledges of what is to come. Hebrews says the patriarchs 'died in faith, without having received the things they were promised,' Hebrews 11:13, and yet God 'is not ashamed to be called their God,' Hebrews 11:16.

For worship, this passage invites us to call on the eternal God in the middle of ordinary business, to trust Him with the long future we cannot secure, and to let His presence with us be visible in our honesty and peace with others.

crossReferences.note: God promised to bless Abraham, make his name great and bless all the families of the earth through him. Abimelech's recognition that 'God is with you in all that you do' is an early sign of that promise at work, as an outsider seeks Abraham's goodwill.

Abimelech and Phicol come to Isaac with nearly the same words, 'We can plainly see that the LORD has been with you,' and swear an oath with him. Isaac's servants find water, he names the well Shibah, and Beersheba's name is confirmed. The promise and its outward signs pass to the next generation.

After Abraham's death the Philistines stopped up his wells, and Isaac's herdsmen fought over new ones until he found room at Rehoboth. The later history shows how fragile Abraham's well rights were, and how the treaty of Genesis 21 was only a partial and temporary security.

God promised an 'everlasting covenant' and 'an eternal possession' of the land. The word for everlasting is the same olam that appears in El Olam. Abraham at Beersheba names God by the very quality that guarantees these promises.

'The LORD is the everlasting God, the Creator of the ends of the earth. He will not grow tired or weary.' Isaiah uses the same title as Genesis 21:33 to comfort exiles who felt forgotten, the same comfort Abraham needed in a land he did not yet own.

'Before the mountains were born... from everlasting to everlasting You are God.' The psalm, attributed to Moses, expands the meaning of El Olam, setting God's eternity against the brevity of human life and making Him the dwelling place of every generation.

Jacob and Laban make a covenant and set up a heap of stones as a witness between them. Like the seven ewe lambs in Genesis 21:30, a physical object serves as legal testimony to an agreement, a common way of sealing treaties in the patriarchal world.

Men from the nations grasp the robe of a Jew, saying, 'Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.' Abimelech's words in Genesis 21:22 foreshadow this prophetic vision of the nations drawn to God's people by His evident presence among them.

By faith Abraham 'dwelt in the promised land as a stranger in a foreign country' and lived in tents, looking for the city whose builder is God. Genesis 21:34, where Abraham 'resided' among the Philistines for a long time, is a snapshot of this pilgrim faith.

At Sarah's death Abraham tells the Hittites, 'I am a foreigner and an outsider among you.' Even after the treaty at Beersheba and many years in the land, the only land he ever owns is a well right and a burial field, which makes his worship of El Olam an act of faith.

Israel's leaders refuse to break an oath made even with deceitful Gibeonites, because they had sworn by the LORD. Oaths with foreign peoples, like Abraham's with Abimelech, were binding before God, and later Scripture shows judgment when such an oath was broken, 2 Samuel 21:1-2.

At Jacob's well Jesus contrasts water that leaves people thirsty again with the water He gives, which becomes 'a fount of water springing up to eternal life.' The patriarchs' wells, secured by oath and quarrel, point to the living water that cannot be taken away.

study.oneStory:
In the story of creation, humanity was placed in a garden watered by a river and given the whole earth to fill, Genesis 2:10. After the fall, the ground was cursed, and the story moved into dry places. The promise to Abraham in Genesis 12 was that God would give his offspring a land and through them bless all nations. By Genesis 21 the promised son has been born, but the land is still in other hands. This passage shows the promise at work in the meantime: a foothold, a well, a peace with neighbours, and worship.

It answers what came before in quiet ways. The man who had lied to Abimelech in chapter 20 now keeps his word to him. The God who had protected Abraham among the nations is now recognised by them. And the promise of blessing for the nations begins to take shape as a foreign king seeks peace with the man of God.

It also sets up what comes after. Beersheba becomes the home of the patriarchs and the southern boundary of Israel, 'from Dan to Beersheba.' Israel's later life in the land would be marked by the same need to live faithfully among neighbours, keep oaths, and worship the eternal God, and by the same danger of turning holy places into idols, as Amos warned. The quarrels over wells anticipate the struggles of a people who would never fully possess what God promised until the Promised One came.

The story reaches its centre in Christ, who is God with us, who makes peace between enemies by His blood, and who gives the water of life. In Him the blessing that began to touch Abimelech reaches the nations. His people live as Abraham did, as pilgrims who worship the eternal God in a land not yet fully theirs.

The new creation brings the story home. The pilgrims receive 'a better country, a heavenly one,' Hebrews 11:16. The city of God has a river of the water of life flowing through it, Revelation 22:1, and no one will need to dig wells, fight over water, or swear oaths for protection. The nations will walk in the light of God, and the Everlasting God will dwell with His people forever. The quiet worship under a tamarisk at Beersheba is a small anticipation of that eternal peace.

quiz.q: Why did Abimelech come to make a treaty with Abraham?

options.text: Because he could see that God was with Abraham in all that he did.
options.note: Abimelech says so directly in verse 22; the blessing of God is what draws him.

options.text: Because he wanted a share of Abraham's flocks and herds.
options.note: Gifts of livestock are exchanged, but the stated reason is that God was with Abraham.

options.text: Because Abraham had threatened him with war.
options.note: Abraham raises a grievance about a well, but there is no threat of war; the treaty is one of peace.

options.text: Because God commanded Abimelech to do so in a dream.
options.note: No such command is given here; Abimelech acts on what he has seen of God's blessing.

quiz.q: What does the name Beersheba signify in this passage?

options.text: Well of the oath or well of seven, marking the oath sworn and the seven lambs given as witness.
options.note: The name ties together the oath and the seven ewe lambs set apart as a witness.

options.text: Simply the place where Abraham camped for a season.
options.note: Abraham does reside there, but the name specifically commemorates the oath and the seven lambs.

options.text: The city Abraham built and fortified.
options.note: Abraham plants a tree and digs a well; he does not build a fortified city.

options.text: The name of the well Abimelech's servants had seized.
options.note: Beersheba names the place of the covenant and oath, not the seized well as such.

quiz.q: How did Abraham respond after the treaty was made?

options.text: He planted a tamarisk tree and called on the LORD, the Everlasting God.
options.note: Abraham marks the peace with an act of worship to El Olam.

options.text: He returned at once to Hebron and built an altar there.
options.note: He worships, but the text says he planted a tree at Beersheba and resided in the land, not that he returned to Hebron.

options.text: He demanded that Abimelech leave the land.
options.note: It is Abraham who resides in the land; there is no such demand.

options.text: He broke the covenant as soon as Abimelech left.
options.note: Abraham keeps the peace and settles there for a long time.

quiz.q: What does the title El Olam, the Everlasting God, emphasise here?

options.text: That God endures forever and so can be trusted to keep His promises across time.
options.note: The Everlasting God is the fitting anchor for a pilgrim holding a long delayed promise.

options.text: That God is powerful enough to win any battle.
options.note: God's power is real, but this title stresses His eternity and permanence rather than might in battle.

options.text: That God lives only in the land of Canaan.
options.note: The title speaks of God's eternity, not a location; He is not bound to one land.

options.text: That God had only recently revealed Himself to Abraham.
options.note: El Olam stresses that God is from everlasting, the opposite of recent or temporary.

quiz.q: How does this small scene fit the larger story of Genesis?

options.text: It shows the promise to bless the nations beginning to bear fruit as a king seeks out Abraham.
options.note: Abimelech's confession echoes the promise of Genesis 12 that nations would be blessed through Abraham.

options.text: It records a minor land dispute with no bearing on the promise.
options.note: There is a dispute, but the scene clearly advances the promise as the nations recognise God's blessing.

options.text: It marks the moment Abraham finally owns all of Canaan.
options.note: Abraham gains only a well and a place; full possession of the land still lies far ahead.

options.text: It shows Abraham abandoning his faith to make a worldly alliance.
options.note: Abraham keeps faith and worships the LORD; the treaty is peace, not compromise.

questions: Abimelech could see that God was with Abraham in everything he did. What would others see about God at work in your ordinary life this week?
Abraham raised his grievance about the well honestly and openly, and it led to peace. Is there a tension you are avoiding that God might want you to address plainly?
Abraham worshipped as a stranger in a land he did not yet own. Where are you being asked to trust and worship God before you can see the promise fulfilled?
Abraham called on God as the Everlasting God. How does knowing that God never changes or grows weary steady you when His promises seem slow?
A pagan king was drawn toward the God of Abraham. Who in your life might be watching, and how could your trust in God open a door for them?

translationNotes.note: Beersheba can mean well of seven or well of the oath; the Hebrew wordplay ties together the seven ewe lambs and the sworn oath, and both senses are in view.
The Hebrew reads El Olam, rendered the Eternal or Everlasting God, a title stressing God's unbounded, age long existence.
